items.title: Bill Holman interviewed by Monk Rowe, Los Angeles, California, February 13, 1999
items.q: a take off on “Keen and Peachy” that Shorty had done for Woody

ctx.x: I think so. So the days of stealing something from Manny Albam or something like that—

Odd you should mention that, because I did that exact thing. When he was writing for Barnet in 1949 I heard them down in Balboa and they played that, what do you call it, “Swell and Super” a thing, a take off on “Keen and Peachy” that Shorty had done for Woody. And I went home and tried to write a chart something like that. But yeah, that’s what you do when you’re young. You try this and you hear something you like and you say I want to try that. And then it just kind of gets absorbed into the whole conception…

In your own band, I’m not sure how to ask this question, has electronics entered into, even in the big band field. Actually what I think I’m getting at is does your rhythm section use electric instruments and if so does it change the sound?

items.title: Holman Bill — Smithsonian Jazz Oral History
items.q: Shorty was great to work with, but a lot of times he left the work to the other people. One time I remember, we were doing a big band date

ctx.x: Okay. Anything you would like to share for the historical record about your Shorty Rogers period and what was he like to work with?

Shorty was great to work with, but a lot of times he left the work to the other people. One time I remember, we were doing a big band date, and he hadn‟t marked any of the notes that were to be played short and which ones to be played long. To me, that‟s very important. So we had to take out an hour and have Al Porcino tell the whole band, make this one short, make this one long. Shorty just stood there, twirling his hair. Talk about mild-mannered. He was the personification of that: never a bad word about…
Then, by August of ‟53, we‟re showing more recordings with Stan Kenton.
